Beállítom Vlagyimir Putyin orosz elnök ellátogatott a Kuril-szigetcsoport egyik déli, Japán által magának követelt szigetére. A látogatásra egy nappal azután került sor, hogy Oroszország nagyszabású haditengerészeti hadgyakorlatot tartott a térségben, valamint szövetségese, Észak-Korea újabb ballisztikus rakétát lőtt ki – írta a Reuters . Oroszország és Japán a mai napig nem kötött hivatalos békeszerződést a második világháború lezárásáról, mert nem tudnak megegyezni a Kuril-szigetek hovatartozásáról. A japán Hokkaidó szigettől az orosz Kamcsatka félszigetig húzódó szigetcsoport Oroszországhoz tartozik, de Japán igényt formál a négy legdélebbi szigetre. Japán ezeket a szigeteket Északi Területeknek nevezi. Ezek közé tartozik a szigetcsoport legnagyobb tagja, a több mint hétezer lakosú Iturup (japánul Etorofu) , ahová most Putyin ellátogatott. A TASZSZ orosz állami hírügynökség beszámolója szerint Putyin mostani útja az első látogatása a Kuril-szigeteken. Az Iturup szigeten felkereste a Jasznij halfeldolgozó üzemet, miután megfigyelte az orosz haditengerészet távol-keleti hadgyakorlatát. Putyin a hadgyakorlat megtekintése során azt mondta: „Kötelességünk az orosz állam biztonságának biztosítása az összes határa mentén, minden régióban.” Japán külügyminisztere az X-en tiltakozott Putyin látogatása miatt. „Az Északi Területek, köztük Etorofu, történelmileg és a nemzetközi jog alapján is Japán elidegeníthetetlen területét képezik. Japán határozottan tiltakozik a látogatás ellen” – írta Motegi Tosimicu. Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! https://www.dw.com/en/a-war-fatigued-and.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Mmmu The upcoming Duma elections are hard to miss when you walk down Moscow's streets Image: Ramil Sitdikov/REUTERS Advertisement Russians are increasingly anxious . Nearly half of those surveyed by state pollster FOM say a sense of alarm is the prevailing mood among the people around them. According to data by independent pollster ExtremeScan , 60% of Russians believe that the war against Ukraine has had negative consequences for their day-to-day lives. "Anxiety and war fatigue are driven by increasing uncertainty," Margarita Zavadskaya, a sociologist and senior research fellow at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs in Helsinki, told DW. She says this year has seen a shift in public opinion. Rising prices, internet crackdowns, fuel shortages caused by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and rumors of another mobilization drive are making it harder for Russians to plan for the future. Some are even leaving the country, afraid they could be drafted after the elections. All 450 seats in the Duma are at stake in the upcoming election Image: Ramil Sitdikov/REUTERS Sociologist and the founder of ExtremeScan Elena Koneva said people were starting to ask the question: "How much does this war cost me and my family? And am I ready to pay this price? " That could pose a problem for the Kremlin . From September 18 to 20, Russians are voting for a new parliament (the State Duma) for the first time since 2022. It's the first parliamentary election to take place in Russia during the Ukraine war. And although there are unlikely to be any surprises in the official results, the Kremlin will be closely monitoring turnout. Why are these elections important for the Kremlin? "The Kremlin is confident it can fabricate whatever figures it needs. The question is how high of a price it will have to pay," said Zavadskaya. Although elections in authoritarian systems like that of Russian President Vladimir Putin have little to do with democratic change, they still serve an important purpose. They are a reality check on whether the population remains loyal. And for Putin, that is especially important right now. "They are crucial for him because they demonstrate that the majority supports the main party, the party of war, and that he has legitimacy for further escalation and the continuation of this war," Russian opposition politician in exile Ilya Yashin told DW. In the fifth year of the war in Ukraine, there is little sign the Kremlin is willing to end the conflict. United Russia, a party de facto led by Putin, is campaigning on a platform that lists victory in the war among its priorities. Its candidate list is headed by people presented as veterans of the war against Ukraine. But many Russians appear to want the opposite. "The silent majority just wants the war to end," opposition politician Yulia Galyamina, who still lives in Russia, said in a recent interview with online media-outlet Bereg . Most of these people still support Putin, but they are becoming increasingly anti-war, she said. That mood is also reflected in polling. Six in 10 Russians favor peace negotiations with Ukraine, according to independent pollster Levada Center . Recent Kremlin hints at a new round of peace talks in October may be a tactic to calm the electorate, Zavadskaya said. Support for Yabloko has been rising One party has sought to capitalize on this anti-war sentiment: Yabloko. The liberal opposition party is the only registered political force opposing the war in Ukraine. Although its rating was below 5% in July, the party has seen a surge in popularity since then. Many people, especially younger Russians, are joining Yabloko and volunteering. Russian court confirms anti-war party election ban To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video According to the independent pollster ExtremeScan, 18% of Russians would have voted for Yabloko. But they will not be able to: In a recent court decision, Yabloko was barred from running in the parliamentary elections. "This support for Yabloko is, in fact, a demonstration of people's attitude toward the war," Koneva told DW. What will anti-war voters do? Now, with Yabloko out of the race, are there still ways for Russians to express that attitude? Yulia Navalnaya , the widow of Alexei Navalny , and opposition politician in exile Maxim Katz are urging supporters to back any party except United Russia in an effort to reduce the ruling party's result in the election. Yabloko has taken a different approach, encouraging voters to spoil their ballots. Yashin says neither choice matters. What matters, he says, is showing up at polling stations at noon on Sept. 20. Navalnaya (center) and Yashin (right) have different suggestions for how voters in Russia can show their discontent with the government (file photo from June 2025) Image: Alexis Haulot/European Union 2025 - Source : EP "These queues will be a visible expression of public discontent," he said. "No need for flags, banners, or symbols. Everyone will know: the queues at noon are made up of people who do not want the war to continue." DW Russian asked its readers anonymously whether they plan to vote in the upcoming election. Most of those who responded said they would follow Navalnaya's and Katz's advice. "Elections have long become a farce and a political spectacle. But I will vote because I want to show that I have a position," one user said. Others decided to stay away from the elections. One respondent wrote: "I don't want to legitimize Putin's regime." Sergei Satanovskii contributed reporting. The demonstration was one of the most visible anti-war protests seen in Russia in recent months. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Houthi fighters pose amid the wreckage of a Saudi F-15 fighter jet that the group claimed to have downed in the province of Marib. Photograph: Houthi Group press Service/UPI/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Houthi fighters pose amid the wreckage of a Saudi F-15 fighter jet that the group claimed to have downed in the province of Marib. Photograph: Houthi Group press Service/UPI/Shutterstock Yemen Up to 169 killed in Yemen as Houthis battle for Red Sea coastal heights Thousands flee fighting as Iran-aligned group seeks to consolidate territorial gains against Saudi-backed government forces Middle East live – latest updates William Christou in Beirut Tue 22 Sep 2026 09.57 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 12.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google As many as 169 people have been reportedly killed in Yemen in the last three days as Iran-aligned Houthis battle Saudi-backed government forces for control of strategic heights on the Red Sea coast, while thousands flee the violence. Houthi military officials said at least 118 people had been killed in clashes as well as Saudi air and artillery strikes on Taiz, al-Jawf, Marib and Saada provinces since Sunday, Agence France-Presse reported. Yemeni government sources have said at least 36 people have been killed on their side of the conflict. The Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of striking the port city of Mocha on Tuesday, killing six civilians, including two children. The group also said a Saudi strike on a prison in al-Jawf province, north-western Yemen, killed nine detainees. The Saudi government, which backs Yemen’s UN-recognised government against Houthi forces, on Tuesday issued an alert in the south of the country before potential strikes, after the Houthis launched strikes at the Saudi capital, Riyadh, at the weekend for the first time in years. View image in fullscreen A screengrab from AFPTV footage of Saudi-backed government fighters engaging Houthi forces in al-Jawf province, in the north-west of Yemen. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images The renewed fighting came after a dramatic offensive launched by the Houthis three weeks earlier in which the group seized control of much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast from government-aligned forces. They were the most significant territorial gains in the last four years of the civil war in the country. The offensive has upended global energy markets, which are already reeling from the Iranian closure of the strait of Hormuz, and further expanded the regional scope of the US-Iran war, now in its seventh month. Last week the Houthis took control of Mocha and other strategic cities, which gave them control over the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key shipping lane home to 10% of all global maritime traffic that has gained renewed importance after the closure of the strait of Hormuz. The clashes have compounded an already dire humanitarian crisis, where about 22 million people need humanitarian assistance and 5.2 million people are already internally displaced. View image in fullscreen Displaced Yemeni people receive medical care at a camp in Ras Imran, a coastal area on the western outskirts of Aden. Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP Yemen’s civil war started in 2014 when the Houthis seized control of the country’s capital and toppled the government. A Saudi-led coalition then intervened in an aerial campaign on behalf of the internationally recognised Yemeni government and allied militias. A UN-brokered ceasefire was established in 2022, which had largely held until the Houthis launched the current offensive. In recent days, clashes have focused on the strategic Kahboub mountains near the Red Sea coast as the Houthis seek to consolidate recent territorial gains. Government forces have been trying to hold the line against the Houthi advance on multiple fronts to prevent them from seizing the mountain range. Control of the mountains would give the Houthis a strategic vantage point over Red Sea coastal areas and would further cut off Aden, the seat of Yemeni government forces, from the western coast. Seizing the mountains would also complicate future government counterattacks. The Houthis have advanced on multiple fronts, particularly the outskirts of Taiz province and the coastal area of Ras al-Ara, with the greater goal of controlling the Kahboub mountains. Media affiliated with the Houthis have reported gains in the area, while government media said its fighters had successfully repelled Houthi incursions. View image in fullscreen Houthi-aligned detainees arrive in Sana’a after being freed from prisons run by Saudi-backed forces in Mocha after Houthis made gains in the region. Photograph: Mohammed Hamoud/Getty Images Since the Houthi campaign was launched, the group has routed government-aligned forces from western Yemen. The prospect of an Iranian-aligned force controlling Bab al-Mandeb has worried Saudi Arabia as it would place two shipping lanes vital to its energy exports in the hands of Iran and its allies. Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes on Yemen in recent days to try to stop the Houthis, with little success. Donald Trump reportedly considered striking the Houthis over the weekend but called them off at the last minute , while the UK said it would assist aerial refuelling of Saudi aircraft engaged in defensive missions, leaving open the prospect of further international intervention. Members of the G7 have called on Iran to stop arming the Houthis. In a joint statement released ahead of the UN general assembly, member states urged the Houthis to stop their strikes on Saudi Arabia, which have damaged key oil infrastructure and wounded dozens. “We call on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions, all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith,” the statement read. The clashes have killed about 700 people and displaced more than 100,000 people, pushing some Yemenis to flee the fighting via sea. Civilians have fled westwards across the Red Sea to Djibouti, while aid groups warn conditions for those remaining in Yemen are deteriorating. View image in fullscreen People fleeing the fighting queue to receive supplies after crossing the Red Sea and arriving in Djibouti. Photograph: Abdourahim Arteh/Reuters Babar Baloch, a UN refugee agency spokesperson, said on Tuesday that displacement inside Yemen could rise to 230,000 people and more than 10,000 could flee to Djibouti if fighting continued. Saudi Arabia has tried to marshal international support to roll back the Houthi offensive, with the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, asking Trump to strike the Houthis – a request Trump has thus far refused. Trump held a call with the head of Yemen’s governing body, Rashad al-Alimi, on Monday, with al-Alimi asking the US for military assistance. Trump expressed solidarity but did not promise military support, a source told Agence France-Presse. https://www.dw.com/en/why-eritrea-matter.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NGTu For Eritrea's President Isaias Afwerki, the end of US sanctions removes one source of international pressure [FILE: February 2023] Image: Khalil Senosi/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement On September 23, fighting escalated dramatically in Ethiopia 's Tigray region. Tigrayan forces seized three local airports and the conflict spread into the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara, according to reports. Both sides have accused the other of starting the escalation. The renewed fighting poses a major challenge to the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement that ended the previous Tigray war. This is where Eritrea becomes crucial. Martin Plaut, a British journalist specializing in the Horn of Africa , noted that the US needs Eritrea in the struggle to secure the Red Sea against the Houthis , an Iran-backed Shiite Muslim militia. Plaut argues that removing sanctions gives new political weight to one of Africa's most repressive regimes. As fighting resumes in Tigray , Eritrea could once again become a decisive military player. Plaut said the current tensions had the potential of developing into a broader regional confrontation, which, he said, "is the most serious danger." Eritrea's location at the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is an asset for the autocratic nation, as partners from near and far seek access to the Red Sea Image: ABACA/picture alliance In his view, the administration of US President Donald Trump has already made a strategic calculation. "Trump has now mended fences with Eritrea and has lifted sanctions against Eritrea" in an effort to reduce the threat posed by the Houthis and secure the Red Sea, said Plaut. A striking coincidence of timing The escalation in Tigray came only days after Washington removed key Eritrean entities and individuals from its sanctions list. On September 18, the United States allowed the national emergency underpinning its Ethiopia-related sanctions regime to expire. The Treasury Department subsequently removed a number of Eritrean individuals and entities from its sanctions list, including senior financial official Hagos Ghebrehiwet and the Red Sea Trading Corporation. The measures had originally been imposed in 2021 in connection with the Tigray war. US officials have not described the move as an endorsement of Eritrea, nor has Washington publicly said that it struck a deal with Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki . But it removes a layer of pressure on a government whose strategic importance has grown as security around the Red Sea deteriorates . For Abdurahman Sayed, director of the Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration and a political analyst, the wider geopolitical context is crucial. "It is happening at a time when the war on Iran is ongoing," he told DW. "The Strait of Hormuz has been blocked for some time , and now the Bab el-Mandeb on the Red Sea, where Eritrea is located — this may give Eritrea some advantage to establish a meaningful relationship with the US." Why Eritrea matters Eritrea controls a long coastline opposite Yemen . Its southern port of Assab lies close to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most important maritime waterways. Moses Okello, a senior researcher at the Institute for Security Studies in Addis Ababa, said the regional context has fundamentally changed since the previous Tigray war. "In 2020, the concern was the TPLF [Tigray People's Liberation Front] versus the Ethiopian National Defense Force [ENDF]," he told DW. "Today, the entire Middle East is up in flames, and now the tensions in the Red Sea. So this changes the strategic value of not just the Eritrean coast, but the entire Red Sea waterway." Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video For Washington, cooperation — or at least non-hostility — from Eritrea can therefore be strategically valuable. But the bargain carries risks. Eritrea is one of the world's most authoritarian states, with no national elections since independence in 1993 and an extensive system of indefinite national service. Eritrean forces also fought alongside Ethiopian federal troops during the 2020-22 Tigray war. And the economic impact of lifting sanctions may be more limited than the political symbolism suggests. "Lifting the sanctions may not make a huge difference on the ground," said Sayed. "Eritrea is not a trade hub [nor does it have] a well-established trading relationship with the outside world. It's actually a closed country." Ethiopia heads back toward war The latest fighting did not emerge from nowhere. On September 21, seven Ethiopian armed and political groups announced an alliance aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. The coalition includes the TPLF, the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army. Some members were on opposing sides during the 2020-22 Tigray war. It remains unclear how closely the alliance's members will coordinate militarily. The alliance brings together groups with very different histories that share opposition to the federal government. Two days later, fighting escalated in Tigray. Tigrayan forces seized airports and fighting spread into neighboring regions. The TPLF has said federal forces attacked first; Addis Ababa has said the TPLF launched the offensive. The renewed fighting has raised questions about the durability of the 2022 Pretoria agreement. Could Eritrea intervene? During the previous Tigray war, Eritrean forces fought alongside Ethiopian federal troops. But relations between Afwerki and Abiy have since deteriorated sharply. One major dispute concerns Ethiopia's demand for reliable access to the Red Sea. Landlocked since Eritrea's independence, Ethiopia regards maritime access as a strategic necessity. Eritrea insists on its sovereignty and has rejected any suggestion that Ethiopia could obtain access through coercion. The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The Ethiopian government has accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups in the new conflict. Eritrea has denied such allegations. There is currently no public evidence that the US sanctions decision was designed to encourage Eritrean military intervention in Ethiopia. Nor is it clear that Eritrea has decided to enter the fighting. But if the Tigray conflict intensifies , Eritrea could see a direct security interest in intervening. That would transform an Ethiopian conflict into a potentially interstate confrontation. A regional conflict waiting to spread The Horn of Africa is already exceptionally volatile. Sudan remains at war. Somalia is unstable. Ethiopia and Egypt remain locked in a dispute over the Nile and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam . Saudi Arabia and the UAE are pursuing their own interests across the Red Sea and Horn of Africa. And the conflict in Yemen is directly connected to the security of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Okello sees the changing Middle East as an additional reason for urgent engagement. "There is no doubt that the conflict in the Middle East now puts a new contextual layer over that primary tension and increases the urgency to engage with both Eritrea and Addis Ababa to try and address this before it becomes a conflagration which makes addressing issues in the Red Sea a lot more difficult," he said. A new Ethiopia-Eritrea confrontation would therefore not happen in isolation. Plaut warned that regional alliances could interact in dangerous ways. "You have the UAE backing the RSF and you have the Saudis backing the Eritreans and the Sudanese Armed Forces," he said. "This could all multiply and you could get one conflict leading into another." That does not mean a general regional war is inevitable. Most governments involved have strong reasons to prevent an uncontrollable escalation. But the number of links between the region's conflicts is increasing. Eritrea and shifting regional dynamics For Eritrea's President Afwerki, the US decision is an opportunity. The end of the sanctions removes one source of international pressure and may give Eritrea greater diplomatic room for maneuver. More importantly, Washington's renewed engagement with Asmara underscores the strategic value of Eritrea's Red Sea position. Why can't Ethiopia and Eritrea be friends? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The more important Eritrea becomes to US and regional security calculations, the greater the danger that strategic interests will overshadow concerns about its authoritarian system and past military interventions. For Ethiopia, the immediate question is whether the renewed fighting can be stopped before it draws in Eritrea. For Washington, the challenge is whether Eritrea can be engaged as a Red Sea security partner without giving the country greater freedom to destabilize its neighbors. Eritrea has spent decades on the margins of international diplomacy, but its location on the Red Sea has long given it strategic significance. With fighting again raging in Tigray, the Houthis threatening the Red Sea and Washington reopening its channel to Asmara, Eritrea could become one of the key players in the Horn of Africa's next chapter. Ekinder Firew in Addis Ababa contributed to this report. https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-13/r.text: Explore the ABC Russian strike on Ukraine-Poland border stirs fears war is on Europe's 'doorstep' Topic: Unrest, Conflict and War Posted Sun 13 Sep 2026 at 10:43pm Sun 13 Sep 2026 at 10:43pm Sun 13 Sep 2026 at 10:43pm , updated Mon 14 Sep 2026 at 9:19am Mon 14 Sep 2026 at 9:19am Mon 14 Sep 2026 at 9:19am Video from a social media post shows the aftermath of Russian drone strike near Ukraine's border with Poland. ( Reuters: Supplied ) In short: A Russian strike on the Ukraine-Poland border just missed a train carrying diplomats, including former British prime minister Boris Johnson. Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha says attacks in proximity to NATO countries is a sign of Russia's escalating campaign of "terror" against the EU and NATO. US President Donald Trump has called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian diesel infrastructure, saying the attacks are causing a global shortage of the fuel. abc.net.au/news/russian-strike-on-ukraine-poland-border-stirs-fears-of-war/107148616 Link copied Share Share article Fresh Russian strikes in proximity to NATO countries have stoked fears among some European leaders that the war between Ukraine and Russia is spilling across borders. A Russian drone hit a passenger train near the Ukraine-Poland border shortly after European diplomats, including former prime ministers of the UK and Sweden, had used the same line. The train, on a route frequently used by foreign delegations returning from Kyiv, was attacked just 2 kilometres from the Polish border on Sunday, local time, Ukraine's railway operator said. No casualties were reported. "This wasn't our train, but the one just minutes after us by the border crossing. It was evacuated as the drone approached and no one was hurt," Carl Bildt, Sweden's former prime minister said on X. A locomotive damaged in a Russian drone attack at Yahodyn railway station near Ukraine's border with Poland. ( AP via Ukrainian Ukrzaliznytsia Railway Company Press Office ) He and other politicians were returning to Europe by train after attending a conference in Kyiv. "It is entirely possible that the Russian drone's intended target was the diplomatic train, which departed the station earlier than scheduled after train timetables were adjusted in real time because of the constant threat of Russian strikes," Ukraine's railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, said on Telegram. Former British prime minister Boris Johnson, who was also on the train that left the station shortly before the strike, condemned the attack as "random and senseless". Earlier on Sunday, a truck less than 1km from Ukraine's border with Poland was also hit, prompting the Dorohusk-Yahodyn crossing point to briefly halt operations, according to border guards. Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the "barbaric" strikes in the small town of Yahodyn were "not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders". "This is Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," he said. A passenger train in Lutsk was also hit in a Russian drone strike over the weekend. ( Reuters: Supplied ) Ukraine operates several border crossings with Poland, through which a significant proportion of the military and humanitarian aid from its allies is delivered to the country. Russia's Defence Ministry said it had targeted infrastructure facilitating military cargoes from Europe in Western Ukraine. Ukraine is dependent on trade and arms shipments from across the Polish, Romanian and Moldovan borders. Russia has begun targeting Ukraine's border crossings with its Western allies in recent weeks, as part of a growing campaign by both sides to erode the other's economic infrastructure more than four years into Russia's invasion. Ukrainian Railways also said that in Volyn — another region bordering Poland — a drone attacked the locomotive of a passenger train just 2km from the Polish border. The company said no-one was injured. Trump tells Zelenskyy to stop hitting Russian diesel US President Donald Trump on Sunday called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian diesel infrastructure, saying the attacks were causing a shortage of the fuel that is "hurting the world". A wave of long-distance Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries in recent months has reduced that country's fuel production, triggering gasoline shortages across the country. Ukraine, which faces regular Russian attacks on its own energy infrastructure, says refineries are legitimate military targets. Donald Trump has clamed a global fuel shortage on the Russia-Ukraine war, rather than the war he started with Iran. ( Reuters via Cathal McNaughton ) The US national average price for diesel, used by trucks, trains, ships, and farm equipment, rose by over $US6 a gallon for the first time on Thursday, according to price tracker GasBuddy. "Mr Zelenskyy has to do one thing: He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Mr Trump told journalists during a visit to Ireland . "We spoke to Mr Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don't hit diesel fuel. That's hurting the world." The global shortage "isn't done by the Middle East; this is done by what's happening with Russia and Ukraine," Mr Trump added. Russia downgraded its oil output forecast for this year to a 17-year low and revised its fuel exports outlook for 2026 and 2027 due to the war, according to a government draft forecast seen by Reuters. Narendra Modi has told Vladimir Putin that the war must end. ( Pyotr Kovalyov via Reuters ) Putin told the war in Ukraine must end In India, where Russian President Vladimir Putin had been attending the BRICS summit , Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that both Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping had offered help brokering a peace settlement, Russian state news agency TASS reported. Last month, at a summit in Kyrgyzstan, Mr Modi told Mr Putin that the war must end, one of several calls for peace by leaders of nations that have traditionally strong relations with Russia. Xi and Putin among biggest winners at BRICS 2026 Here is everything you need to know about BRICS 2026. Last month, Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev publicly told Mr Putin that he should halt the conflict along the front line, which has remained largely static this year. Russia has ruled that out, saying Ukraine should pull back to leave the industrialised eastern Donbas region in Moscow's hands, something Kyiv has said it will never do. Both Brazil and China, themselves founding BRICS members, have called for a resumption of peace talks. TASS cited Mr Peskov as saying that Mr Putin had informed Mr Modi of the situation "on the ground" in Ukraine, and that Russia had not ruled out resuming three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States in October. Ukraine strikes nuclear power plant in Russian-held territories Overnight, hostilities showed no signs of letting up. In the Russian-held part of Ukraine's south-eastern Zaporizhzhia region, the head of Russia's state nuclear energy company, Rosatom, accused Ukraine of striking fuel trucks near the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power station, Europe's largest. Russia currently controls the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant in southern Ukraine. ( Reuters: Alina Smutko ) Russia has controlled the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant since March 2022, and it remains close to the front line. A Ukrainian military spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In Russia itself, the mayor of the city of Nizhnekamsk, in the Volga River region of Tatarstan, said that "civilian and industrial" targets in the city had been struck by Ukrainian drones, causing at least two deaths and several more injuries. Mayor Radmir Belyaev did not clarify which targets were struck, but the city hosts a major oil refinery that has been attacked before. Ukrainian authorities did not immediately comment on the strike on Nizhekamsk, but did say they had struck another refinery in the southern Krasnodar region. Lithuania also briefly closed Vilnius airport on Sunday, after a possible drone sighting prompted NATO to scramble at least one fighter jet, the National Crisis Management Centre said. Lithuania later said the sighting turned out to be a flock of birds. Military drones straying into the airspace of Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are stoking concerns that the war in Ukraine is spilling over into NATO's northern borders with Russia. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Illustration: Nathalie Lees/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Illustration: Nathalie Lees/The Guardian Opinion Housing The housing crisis is now global. It shows just how undemocratic our nations have become Leilani Farha When we can’t even afford to rent or buy somewhere to live, we have to ask: did we give the financial sector too much power? Leilani Farha is the former UN special rapporteur on adequate housing Mon 19 Oct 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 03.15 EDT Share I n the summer of 2021, I visited a homeless community in a park in Toronto, Canada, and spoke to one of the residents. He was living in a tent in the shadow of brand new skyscrapers, and had been homeless for about five years. At one point he swivelled around, pointed up at a crane on the skyline, and said: “Who are they building those for? Definitely not for me.” He was right. And he captured something experienced by ordinary people around the world: the growing conviction that the housing system is no longer tethered to their needs. What he was pointing at is not just a housing crisis. It is a crisis of democracy. Democracy promises that our living conditions are shaped by all of us, regardless of our station in life. Yet decisions about housing have been systematically removed from democratic control and handed to financial actors such as private equity firms, pension funds and real-estate investment trusts. Working hand in hand with governments and banks, these actors have decoupled the price of housing from what ordinary people earn. They’ve transformed our homes into a toy for wealthy investors. I call this alliance Housing Inc. The tools available to the large financial actors driving and profiting from the housing crisis are not available to the rest of us. They hire armies of lobbyists to squash rent-control laws. They fund political campaigns. They rotate in and out of government positions. They are in the rooms and hallways where decisions are made. Even governments trying to fight the growing influence of the financial sector in housing face intense pressure. In Copenhagen, after the private equity giant Blackstone bought up apartment blocks across the city, renovated them and, in some cases, doubled the rent for new tenants, the Danish parliament passed legislation barring new owners from raising rents on renovated apartments for five years. While this “ Blackstone law ”, as it was commonly called, was a brave measure, it was weaker than the government had wanted. Kaare Dybvad, then Denmark’s housing minister, had proposed a 10-year freeze. Faced with fury from landlords and pension funds, and needing rightwing party votes to pass it, he cut it to five. The average tenant, the person experiencing homelessness, the young person locked out of the housing market – what do they have? They have a vote. That is all. And the vote changes less than we are promised. As the economist Yanis Varoufakis has argued , elections no longer determine economic policy. Governments of the left and the right come and go, and regardless of who is in power, rents keep rising, because the economic model always stays the same: money flows to wherever the returns are highest, which means into unproductive assets such as real estate, and away from the public investment that would actually house people. We can change our governments. We cannot, it seems, change the economic policies they all adhere to. Who decided that financial firms could use our homes as investments? Not the public. Consider the bundling of mortgages into securities, which laid the groundwork for the 2008 financial crisis, or the decision in more than 40 jurisdictions to exempt real-estate investment trusts from corporate income tax. Both happened out of public view, shaped by governments and financial actors, with no public debate. The same thing happens with other kinds of housing investment. Take short-term rentals in Athens. While democracy may have been born there, it hasn’t always thrived. After the global financial crisis, Greeks were held to brutal austerity measures against their will. Property values collapsed, wages fell and ordinary families struggled to make ends meet. For many property owners, renting to tourists through short-let platforms such as Airbnb became a lifeline – a way to generate income from an asset that had lost most of its value. But what began as a survival strategy for families became an investment strategy for foreign buyers. The government introduced a “golden visa” programme in 2013, offering residency to any foreigner who bought Greek property. Thousands did – not to live there, but to convert apartments into short-term rentals, banking on Greece’s tourism industry as a good investment. As foreign capital flooded in, long-term housing became scarcer, rents spiked and neighbourhoods such as Exarchia and Koukaki began to change beyond recognition.Athenians protested and their government responded by sending in the riot police and steamrollering dissent to defend its decisions. What’s on offer in terms of genuine civic engagement for the people most affected by the housing crisis tends to be defanged, inadequate or inaccessible. Tenants who speak out about poor conditions risk eviction, and they need landlord references for their next place. People holding down multiple jobs just to pay their rent don’t have time for city council meetings, or surveys and questionnaires that lead nowhere. When people have no means to participate in decisions about their own housing, they feel abandoned by government. This creates a vacuum that rightwing populism is perfectly designed to fill. Which brings us back to democracy’s promise. Can it be a democracy when a place to live is governed not by human beings and their needs but by financial firms and profit, pricing people out of their homes and onto the streets? Around the world, people are forcing that question into the open. In Madrid, 87-year-old María del Carmen Abascal (better known as Maricarmen) had lived in the same flat for 71 years when the investment firm that owns it demanded she pay €2,650 (£2,280) a month instead of €500. On 23 September, after earlier attempts had been blocked, police cleared hundreds of her neighbours from the doorway and she was evicted. That evening, thousands took to the streets of Madrid. Within days there were tens of thousands, a protest camp had filled the Puerta del Sol square, and demonstrations had spread to cities across the country. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more after newsletter promotion Six days after the eviction, the Spanish government passed emergency decrees extending rental contracts and shielding vulnerable tenants from eviction. People called it the “Maricarmen decree”. Three days later, parliament struck it down . The parties of the right had voted against it, one of them calling automatic lease renewal an “expropriation of property rights”. Maricarmen passed away not long after. In Berlin in 2021, more than one million people – 59.1% of valid votes – backed a referendum to take the homes owned by the city’s largest corporate landlords into public ownership. The result was non-binding, and successive governments have ignored it. So Berliners used the one tool they had, blunt as it was. On 20 September this year, Die Linke, which had campaigned on the promise to carry out the referendum, won the state elections and became the largest party in the city’s parliament for the first time. One day later, before a government had even been formed, Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, announced that he would fast-track a national law banning the “expropriation” of housing. Berliners had voted for a change in economic policy on housing, and the chancellor then made it clear that this was not theirs to decide. But the movement had known better than to rely on the broken promise of democracy. Last year, it wrote an expropriation law itself, so that it could be passed by a willing government – or, failing that, put to a second, binding vote. In its own words: “ Allet mussma selba machn ” – we have to do everything ourselves. That is what it takes to reclaim democracy. Leilani Farha is the 2026 CBC Massey lecturer. This piece is based on her new book: Housing Inc.: A Global Takeover and Our Fight for Home .
